newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn seen winning Bundesbank's EMU blessing.
newsitem.headline: Bonn seen winning Bundesbank's EMU blessing.

text.p: The Bundesbank, champion of strict financial discipline, is likely to look the other way if Germany fails to meet precisely all the criteria for joining the European single currency, analysts said on Wednesday.

Despite the rhetoric of some Bundesbank officials, the central bank council as a whole would not be worried if Germany narrowly missed in 1997 meeting the budget deficit goals set in the Maastricht treaty, economists said.
The council is likely to take a longer-term view of the country's broader economic fundamentals, they added.

"The struggle over numerical targets is down to semantics," said Adolf Rosenstock, economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan. "From an economic standpoint the Bundesbank is not worried about Bonn's missing the target by a moderate amount."

The powerful German central bank, however, will likely not take such a kindly view of other nations asking for flexible interpretations of Maastricht and could flex its muscles in financial markets to ensure that an EMU launch goes ahead only on its own terms.

At issue is Germany's ability to reduce its budget deficit to the Maastricht target of three percent of gross domestic product as a condition for joining European monetary union(EMU), scheduled to start in 1999.

Many private economists doubt that Bonn will be able to meet that goal in the target year of 1997. They expect the government to take advantage of vague wording in the treaty to say it meets deficit targets, even if the debt ratio is as high as 3.4 percent.

The Bundesbank, in vague wording of its own, has campaigned for years against what it calls a "flexible interpretation" of treaty rules. But economists said that when push comes to shove the central bank would not raise any objections to Bonn using grey areas of the Maastricht Treaty.

"The council is split, but there are many members of the Bundesbank council who are not worried about the details of the budget criteria," said Holger Schmieding, senior economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt. "In the end, the entire institution will not come out against EMU based on the deficit."

Economists said that from the Bundesbank's point of view, more important than hitting an abitrary economic goal, nations joining monetary union need to have developed a "culture of stability" which already clearly exists in Germany.
"The deficit will be no worse for the euro than it has been for the mark," Stefan Schneider, economist at Paribas Capital Markets, said of the continued strength of the German currency.
The German central bank's biggest concern, analysts said, is to ensure that only nations with a proven track record are allowed to join in 1999.

Although Bonn should be allowed some fiscal latitude, others, namely Italy, should not be allowed into EMU no matter how closely they come to meeting the Maastricht goals in the 1997 snapshot test, analysts said.

Rome may have made great strides in bringing down inflation, cutting its deficit and other criteria needed to join EMU. But analysts said the Bundesbank still is not convinced that Italy is ready for EMU over the long haul.

Although the decision as to who can join the first group of nations to form monetary union in 1999 will be made by political leaders, the Bundesbank holds several very powerful cards which it can play to shape what form EMU will take.

Analysts said the central bank could take advantage of its clout in financial markets either by public comments or by nudging up interest rates, to keep bond yields between Italy and Germany from converging in the second half of the year.
Widening bond yields would give German political leaders ammunition to keep Italy out of EMU at a meeting to decide on EMU membership in spring 1998, economists said.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, meanwhile, could use his position on the governing council of the European Monetary Institute, the precursor of a planned European central bank, to make it hard for Italy and others such as Spain or Portugal to be allowed into EMU, they said.
